q: What is Ansible and how does its agentless architecture work?
a: Ansible is an automation tool for configuration management, application deployment and orchestration. A control node reads an inventory of target hosts and a playbook, which is a YAML description of desired state. For each task it generates a small module, copies it to the target over SSH or WinRM, runs it with the target's Python interpreter, collects the JSON result and removes the temporary files. Because nothing permanent is installed, there is no agent to patch, no extra port to open and no central server required, which makes onboarding fast and the attack surface small. The trade-offs are that SSH round trips cost time at large scale, the control node needs network reach to every host, and Python is needed on managed Linux hosts. Modules are designed to be idempotent, so running the same playbook twice should change nothing the second time.
f: What does a module run look like on the target?
When would you choose an agent-based tool instead?
p: A control node pushes small modules over SSH or WinRM, runs them, returns JSON and cleans up. No agent is installed, which keeps onboarding easy and the attack surface small, at the cost of SSH latency at very large scale.
tip: Say agentless plus idempotent modules, and name the scale trade-off.

q: What is an inventory, and how do static and dynamic inventories differ?
a: An inventory tells Ansible which hosts exist and how they are grouped. A static inventory is an INI or YAML file listing hosts and groups, with variables attached to hosts or groups. It is simple, readable and ideal for stable environments. A dynamic inventory is produced at run time by an inventory plugin or script that queries a source of truth, such as AWS EC2, Azure, GCP, VMware, OpenStack or a CMDB, so the host list follows reality as instances come and go. Plugins usually build groups from tags, regions or other metadata with keyed groups and compose variables. In practice I combine them: dynamic sources for cloud fleets, static files for fixed infrastructure, and a directory containing both. I keep group_vars and host_vars beside the inventory, and use ansible-inventory with the graph or list options to verify what Ansible sees before running anything.
f: How do keyed groups work in a cloud inventory plugin?
How do you verify what an inventory resolves to?
p: Static inventories are files listing hosts and groups; dynamic inventories use plugins to query AWS, Azure, VMware or a CMDB at run time. Combine both in a directory and check results with ansible-inventory.
tip: Say you verify with ansible-inventory before any run.

q: When do you use ad-hoc commands rather than playbooks?
a: Ad-hoc commands run a single module against a set of hosts from the command line, with no file to write. They are ideal for quick, one-off operational tasks: checking connectivity with the ping module, gathering facts, checking disk space, restarting a service on a few hosts during an incident, copying a file, or testing that a new module and credentials work. Anything that should be repeated, reviewed, versioned or run by someone else belongs in a playbook, because playbooks document intent, can be code reviewed, are repeatable across environments and support handlers, loops, conditionals and variables. My rule is that an ad-hoc command is fine for investigation and for emergencies, but if I run the same command twice I turn it into a playbook or role. I also take care with the command and shell modules ad hoc, since they are not idempotent and I prefer purpose-built modules.
f: Why avoid shell in ad-hoc commands?
How would you restart a service on 5 hosts quickly and safely?
p: Ad-hoc commands suit quick investigation or incident actions with one module. Repeatable or shared work goes into a playbook, which is reviewable, versioned and supports variables, handlers and conditionals.
tip: Say if you run it twice, it becomes a playbook.

q: What does idempotency mean in Ansible and how do you keep tasks idempotent?
a: Idempotency means running a task repeatedly leads to the same end state, and a second run reports no changes. Most core modules achieve this by describing desired state, for example the package module with state present, the file module with a mode, or the service module with state started. Each checks current state first and acts only if different. It matters because it makes playbooks safe to rerun, supports drift correction, and lets you trust the changed count as a signal. Problems arise with the command, shell and raw modules, which always report changed unless told otherwise. I fix that with creates or removes arguments, changed_when and failed_when conditions, or by replacing them with proper modules. I also verify by running twice in CI and expecting zero changes on the second run, and use check mode with diff to preview. Non-idempotent tasks hide real drift and cause noisy handlers.
f: How do you make a shell task report changed correctly?
How would you test idempotency in CI?
p: Idempotent tasks converge to the same state on every run, so a second run reports zero changes. Prefer state-based modules, use creates, changed_when and failed_when for command tasks, and test by running twice.
tip: Mention the run-twice test in CI.

q: How does Ansible compare with Puppet, Chef and Terraform, and where does each fit?
a: Ansible is agentless and push-based, uses YAML and is easy to start with, so it is strong for orchestration, ad-hoc operations and configuration of existing machines. Puppet and Chef use agents that pull configuration from a server on a schedule, with a declarative language in Puppet and Ruby-based recipes in Chef, which gives continuous enforcement and drift correction at large scale but needs infrastructure to run. Terraform is different in kind: it provisions and manages the lifecycle of infrastructure resources such as networks, instances and managed services, tracking them in state, while Ansible is better at what happens inside the machine afterwards. A common pattern is Terraform to create infrastructure and Ansible to configure it, or to bake images with Packer and Ansible. There is overlap, since Ansible has cloud modules and Terraform has provisioners, so I choose by the lifecycle: create and destroy with Terraform, configure and operate with Ansible.
f: Why not use Ansible for all provisioning?
What is the drawback of a pull-based agent model?
p: Ansible is agentless, push-based and strong for orchestration and configuration. Puppet and Chef are agent-based pull tools with continuous enforcement. Terraform manages infrastructure lifecycle with state; use it to create, and Ansible to configure.
tip: Say Terraform creates, Ansible configures.

q: How does Ansible choose configuration, and what is the precedence of ansible.cfg?
a: Ansible reads settings from several places, and the first match wins rather than merging. The order is the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable, then ansible.cfg in the current directory, then a hidden ansible.cfg in the user's home, then the system file in etc. Individual settings can also be overridden by environment variables such as ANSIBLE_FORKS and by command line flags, which take priority. Because the current directory file is picked up, a project-level ansible.cfg checked into the repository makes behaviour reproducible for the team and in CI, including the inventory path, roles path, remote user, forks, pipelining, callbacks and the collections path. One security detail: Ansible ignores a configuration file in a world-writable directory, to prevent hijacking. I use ansible-config dump with the only-changed option to see which values are in effect and where they came from, which is the fastest way to debug surprising behaviour.
f: Why is a world-writable ansible.cfg ignored?
How do you see the effective configuration?
p: The first config found wins: ANSIBLE_CONFIG, then ansible.cfg in the current directory, home, then system. Environment variables and flags override. Keep a project ansible.cfg in the repo and inspect with ansible-config dump.
tip: Mention a repo-level ansible.cfg for reproducibility.

q: What are facts, and when would you disable or customise fact gathering?
a: Facts are system information that Ansible collects from each host at the start of a play using the setup module, such as operating system, distribution, network interfaces, memory and mounts. They are available as variables, for example ansible_facts distribution or ansible_default_ipv4, and let playbooks adapt to different platforms. Gathering costs a round trip and a second or more per host, which is significant at scale. I disable it with gather_facts false when a play needs none, or limit it with gather_subset to only what I use, such as min or network. Fact caching with a backend like Redis or JSON files avoids recomputing across runs. I can also write custom facts as files on the host in the facts.d directory, which Ansible exposes under ansible_local, useful for exposing application or compliance data. I prefer the ansible_facts dictionary over injected top-level variables for clarity.
f: How does fact caching speed up large runs?
What are local facts?
p: Facts are host details gathered by the setup module at play start and used as variables. Disable them or limit with gather_subset to save time, cache them for large fleets, and add custom facts under facts.d.
tip: Say gather_subset and caching are the scale levers.

q: How do connection methods and privilege escalation (become) work?
a: Ansible connects through a connection plugin: SSH by default for Linux and network devices using paramiko or OpenSSH, WinRM or SSH for Windows, local for the control node, and docker or kubectl style plugins for containers. Authentication is normally by SSH keys through an agent, with the remote user set in inventory, config or play. Privilege escalation is controlled by become: when true, tasks run through sudo by default, or su, doas and others, as the become user, root unless specified, and the become password can be supplied or sudo can be passwordless for the automation account. I set become at play level only where needed rather than globally, and use become_user for application accounts. Good practice is a dedicated automation user, key-based authentication, restricted sudoers entries where feasible, and a bastion through ProxyCommand or ansible_ssh_common_args when hosts are in private networks.
f: How would you reach hosts behind a bastion?
What is the risk of passwordless sudo for all commands?
p: Connection plugins such as SSH or WinRM reach hosts; become escalates with sudo or su. Use a dedicated automation user with keys, apply become only where needed, and use a bastion through ProxyCommand for private networks.
cmds:
- hosts: db
  become: true
  become_user: postgres
tip: Say least privilege: become only on tasks that need it.

q: What is the difference between modules, plugins and collections?
a: A module is a unit of work that runs on the target host, such as copy, apt, user or service, and returns structured results. A plugin extends Ansible itself and runs on the control node: connection plugins, lookup plugins, filter plugins, callback plugins, inventory plugins and strategy plugins, among others. So modules do the managed work, while plugins change how Ansible connects, reads data, formats output or processes variables. A collection is a distribution format that bundles modules, plugins, roles, playbooks and documentation under a namespace, for example amazon.aws or kubernetes.core, versioned and installed from Galaxy, Automation Hub or a private source. Since ansible-core 2.10 most content lives in collections, so the core package stays small and content releases independently. In playbooks I use fully qualified collection names like ansible.builtin.copy to avoid ambiguity, and pin collection versions in requirements.yml for reproducible runs.
f: Where do lookup plugins run?
Why pin collection versions?
p: Modules run on targets and do the work. Plugins run on the control node and extend connections, lookups, filters and callbacks. Collections package modules, plugins and roles under a namespace and are versioned and pinned in requirements.yml.
tip: Say modules run on targets, plugins on the controller.

q: What is the difference between ansible-core and the Ansible community package, and how do you manage versions?
a: Ansible-core is the engine: the command line tools, the language, the built-in collection and the plugin framework. The community Ansible package, sometimes called the batteries-included distribution, bundles ansible-core with a curated set of collections, so a single install gives you many modules. Red Hat's Ansible Automation Platform is a supported product with certified collections, execution environments and a controller. Version management matters because modules and syntax change: each ansible-core release supports a range of Python versions on the control node and on targets, and old targets may need an older interpreter. I pin ansible-core and collection versions in a requirements file, ideally packaged in an execution environment container image, so laptops, CI and the controller all run the same versions. Upgrades are tested in a branch with ansible-lint and Molecule, and I read the porting guides before moving to a new major release.
f: What breaks when upgrading ansible-core?
Why use an execution environment image?
p: Ansible-core is the engine and built-ins; the community package adds many collections. Pin ansible-core and collection versions, ideally in an execution environment image, and test upgrades with lint and Molecule before rollout.
tip: Say pin versions and package them in an execution environment.

q: Describe the structure of a playbook, plays and tasks.
a: A playbook is a YAML file containing a list of plays. Each play maps a group of hosts to a set of tasks and defines settings such as the remote user, become, variables, gather_facts and tags. Within a play, execution is ordered: pre_tasks, then roles, then tasks, then post_tasks, with handlers notified along the way and run at defined points. Each task calls one module with arguments, may have a name, conditions, loops, register, tags, delegation, error handling and notify. Tasks run in order against all hosts in the play in parallel, up to the forks limit, using the linear strategy by default, so every host completes a task before the next starts. Good style is to give every task a descriptive name, keep plays short by moving logic into roles, use fully qualified module names, keep YAML valid and indent consistently, and put variables in group_vars rather than inside the play.
f: In what order do pre_tasks, roles and tasks run?
What does the linear strategy mean?
p: A playbook is a list of plays; each play targets hosts, sets options and runs pre_tasks, roles, tasks and post_tasks in order. Tasks call modules, run across hosts in parallel, and notify handlers. Keep plays short and named.
cmds:
- name: Configure web
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: nginx
        state: present
tip: Say name every task and push logic into roles.

q: How do handlers work and what are the pitfalls?
a: Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by another task that reported a change, typically to restart or reload a service after its configuration file changed. Multiple notifications of the same handler result in a single run, and handlers run at the end of the play by default, in the order they are defined, not the order they were notified. This design avoids restarting a service several times. Pitfalls include a handler not running because the notifying task failed before the end of the play, since by default a failure stops the flow and skips handlers unless force_handlers is set. Another is needing the restart earlier, in the middle of a play, which you handle with the meta flush_handlers task. Handlers also only fire on change, so a first run that fails halfway can leave a changed file with no restart on the next run, and listen topics allow one notification to trigger several handlers.
f: Why might a handler not run after a failure?
How do you force a handler to run mid-play?
p: Handlers run once at the end of a play when notified by changed tasks, in definition order. Use meta flush_handlers to run earlier, force_handlers to run after failures, and listen to group handlers.
cmds:
- name: Update config
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: app.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/app.conf
  notify: Restart app
tip: Mention flush_handlers and the failed-play pitfall.

q: How do loops work in Ansible, and when should you avoid them?
a: The loop keyword repeats a task over a list, exposing each element as the item variable, which can be renamed with loop_control and loop_var. Loops can iterate over simple lists, lists of dictionaries, dictionaries converted with the dict2items filter, or results from lookups and filters such as subelements and product. You can add labels to keep output readable, a pause for rate limits, and an index variable. Older with_ keywords still work but loop is preferred. I avoid loops when the module already accepts a list, for example the package module accepts many names in one call, which is much faster since it runs once rather than once per item. Another problem is loops with register, which return a results list, and large loops over big data in Jinja, which are slow. Also nested loops in included tasks need loop_var set to avoid clashes with the outer item.
f: Why does loop_var matter in nested includes?
How do you loop over a dictionary?
p: Use loop with item, loop_control for labels and renamed variables, dict2items for dictionaries. Avoid loops where a module accepts a list, such as package, since one call is faster than many.
cmds:
- name: Create users
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: "{{ item.name }}"
    groups: "{{ item.groups }}"
  loop: "{{ users }}"
  loop_control:
    label: "{{ item.name }}"
tip: Say pass a list to the module instead of looping where possible.

q: How do conditionals with when and failed_when and changed_when work?
a: The when keyword runs a task only if a Jinja2 expression is true, written without double curly braces, for example when ansible_os_family equals Debian, or when a registered variable is defined or contains a string. Conditions can combine with and, or and not, and a list of conditions means all must be true. On loops, when is evaluated per item. The failed_when keyword overrides what counts as a failure, useful when a command returns a nonzero code that is acceptable or prints an error message with a zero exit code. Similarly changed_when controls whether the task reports a change, which is essential for making command and shell tasks idempotent and for accurate handler notification. Common mistakes include comparing strings and booleans loosely, forgetting that variables from the command line are strings, and using when with an undefined variable without the default filter. I also use the is defined, is changed and is failed tests for clarity.
f: How do you treat a registered result as failed on certain output?
Why do command-line booleans cause problems?
p: when runs a task on a true expression; failed_when and changed_when redefine failure and change for tasks such as command. Use defaults for undefined variables and watch for string versus boolean types.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/check_app
  register: r
  failed_when: "'CRITICAL' in r.stdout"
  changed_when: false
tip: Say changed_when false for read-only commands.

q: How do you handle errors with block, rescue and always, and ignore_errors?
a: A block groups tasks so they share conditions, privilege settings and error handling. The rescue section runs if any task in the block fails, similar to catch, and the always section runs regardless, similar to finally. The pattern lets you attempt a risky operation, such as a deployment, roll back in rescue, and always send a notification or clean up in always. After a successful rescue the play continues for that host and the host is not marked failed, though the failure is shown in the output. The ignore_errors keyword simply continues past a failing task but hides real problems, so I use it sparingly and prefer targeted failed_when conditions. Related controls are any_errors_fatal to stop all hosts on a failure, max_fail_percentage for rolling deployments, and ignore_unreachable. Inside rescue, the ansible_failed_task and ansible_failed_result variables describe what failed, which helps with diagnostics.
f: What variables are available inside rescue?
When would you use any_errors_fatal?
p: block groups tasks; rescue handles failures and always runs regardless, like try, catch and finally. Prefer this and targeted failed_when over ignore_errors, and use any_errors_fatal or max_fail_percentage for rolling changes.
tip: Say rescue for rollback, always for cleanup.

q: How are tags used, and what are the best practices?
a: Tags label tasks, blocks, roles and plays so you can run or skip a subset of a playbook with the tags and skip-tags options, for example only configuration changes or only the deployment step. Special tags include always, which runs unless skipped explicitly, and never, plus tagged, untagged and all. Tags applied to a role or an include are inherited by the contained tasks differently depending on whether it is a static import or dynamic include, which is a frequent source of confusion: with include_role you need the apply keyword to pass tags to the inner tasks. Best practice is a small, documented vocabulary such as packages, config, deploy and security, rather than ad-hoc tags, and using list-tags to document them. I do not rely on tags for safety, because a partial run may leave things inconsistent, and full runs in CI remain the source of truth. Tags are great for fast iteration during development.
f: How do tags behave with include_role?
What does the always tag do?
p: Tags let you run or skip subsets with --tags and --skip-tags. Imports inherit tags, dynamic includes need apply. Keep a small documented tag vocabulary and rely on full runs in CI.
tip: Mention the import versus include difference.

q: What do delegate_to, run_once and local_action do, and when do you use them?
a: The delegate_to keyword runs a task on a different host than the one being iterated, while still using the original host's variables. It is used for actions that must happen elsewhere: removing a host from a load balancer from the control node before updating it, updating a DNS record through an API, or registering with a monitoring server. With delegate_to localhost, tasks run on the control node, and local_action is a shorthand for that. The run_once keyword executes a task a single time for the whole play, on the first host in the batch, for example one database migration or sending one notification, and the result is shared with all hosts. Cautions are that run_once with serial applies per batch, that delegated tasks use facts of the original host unless delegate_facts is set, and that connection and become settings apply to the delegate target, so credentials must work there.
f: How does run_once behave with serial?
What is delegate_facts?
p: delegate_to runs a task on another host while keeping the current host's variables, for load balancer, DNS or monitoring calls. run_once executes a task once per play or batch. Watch serial interactions and delegated credentials.
cmds:
- name: Drain from LB
  ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: "https://lb/api/drain/{{ inventory_hostname }}"
    method: POST
  delegate_to: localhost
tip: Say run_once applies per serial batch.

q: How do check mode and diff mode work, and what are their limits?
a: Check mode, enabled with the check option, simulates a run: modules that support it report what would change without changing anything. Diff mode, enabled with the diff option, shows a before and after comparison for files and templates. Together they give a dry run for review, useful in change approval and in pull request pipelines. The limits are important: modules that do not support check mode are skipped or report nothing, command and shell tasks are skipped by default unless a check_mode override is set, and later tasks that depend on earlier changes or registered output may fail or show misleading results because the earlier change never happened. You can mark a task with check_mode true or false to force behaviour, for example to run a read-only command even in check mode. So check mode is a strong signal rather than a guarantee, and I still verify in a staging environment before production.
f: Why do some tasks fail only in check mode?
How do you force a command to run in check mode?
p: Check mode simulates changes and diff mode shows file differences, giving a reviewable dry run. Limits include modules without support, skipped command tasks and dependent tasks, so treat it as a signal, not a guarantee.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.command: cat /etc/app.conf
  check_mode: false
  changed_when: false
tip: Say dry-run is advisory; staging remains the proof.

q: What is the difference between command, shell, raw and script modules?
a: The command module runs a command without a shell, so pipes, redirects, environment expansion and operators do not work, which also makes it safer against injection. The shell module runs through a shell, supporting pipes and redirects, with more risk if variables contain untrusted input. The raw module sends the command straight over SSH without needing Python on the target, useful for bootstrapping a host that lacks Python or for network devices. The script module copies a local script to the target and runs it there. None of them is idempotent by default, so each always reports changed unless you use creates or removes, changed_when or failed_when. My order of preference is: a dedicated module first, then command, then shell only when a shell feature is truly required, and then I quote variables carefully with the quote filter. Raw is used only for bootstrap, such as installing Python.
f: When is raw appropriate?
How do you protect shell tasks from injection?
p: command runs without a shell and is safer; shell allows pipes but risks injection; raw needs no Python and suits bootstrapping; script copies and runs a local script. Prefer proper modules and make these idempotent with creates, removes and changed_when.
tip: Say a module first, then command, shell last.

q: What is the difference between include and import for tasks and roles?
a: Imports are static: the import_tasks and import_role statements are processed when the playbook is parsed, so the content is pre-loaded, tags and conditionals are applied to every contained task, and you can list all tasks with list-tasks. Includes are dynamic: include_tasks and include_role are processed when execution reaches them, so file names and loops can use runtime variables, and the included content is not visible to list-tasks. When a condition is attached, with an import it is copied to each inner task, with an include it is evaluated once and gates the whole include. Tags behave differently too: tags on an include apply to the include itself unless you use apply. I use imports for fixed structure because they are predictable, and includes when the file or role depends on facts, loops or conditions known only at run time. Mixing them without understanding this causes skipped tasks and tag surprises.
f: Which one supports looping?
Why might tags seem to be ignored on an include?
p: Import is static, processed at parse time, applying tags and conditions to inner tasks. Include is dynamic, evaluated at run time, so it supports loops and variable file names. Use imports for fixed structure and includes for runtime decisions.
tip: Say static for structure, dynamic for runtime choices.

q: What is the structure of an Ansible role and why use roles?
a: A role is a standard directory layout for reusable automation. Key directories are tasks with main.yml as the entry point, handlers, defaults for low-precedence variables meant to be overridden, vars for high-precedence internal values, templates for Jinja2 files, files for static files, meta for dependencies and metadata, and optionally library, module_utils and tests. Roles let you package one capability, such as an nginx setup or a hardening baseline, and reuse it across playbooks, teams and environments with different variables. They improve readability because playbooks become short lists of roles, enable testing in isolation with Molecule, and can be shared through collections or Galaxy. Good practice is one role per clear responsibility, a documented README with variables, defaults for everything configurable, prefixing variable names with the role name to avoid collisions, no hidden dependencies, and idempotent, platform-aware tasks.
f: Why prefix variables with the role name?
What belongs in defaults versus vars?
p: A role has tasks, handlers, defaults, vars, templates, files and meta. It packages one capability for reuse and isolated testing. Keep one responsibility, document variables, prefix names and put overridable values in defaults.
tip: Say prefix variables to avoid collisions.

q: How do role dependencies work and what are their pitfalls?
a: Dependencies are declared in the role's meta main file as a list of other roles that must run first, optionally with parameters. When the playbook applies the role, Ansible executes the dependencies before it, and by default each dependency runs only once even if several roles list it, unless allow_duplicates is set. They are useful for shared prerequisites such as a common baseline or a repository setup role. Pitfalls include hidden coupling that makes a role harder to understand and test alone, ordering surprises when dependencies pull in tasks the playbook author did not expect, variable precedence changes because dependency parameters are applied as role variables, and difficulty when a dependency comes from another collection. Many teams prefer explicit composition: the playbook lists roles in order, or a higher-level role uses include_role, so the flow is visible. I keep dependencies minimal, documented and version-pinned in requirements.yml.
f: What does allow_duplicates do?
Why prefer explicit role ordering in the playbook?
p: Dependencies in meta main run before a role and execute once by default unless allow_duplicates is set. They hide coupling and affect variable precedence, so keep them minimal and often compose roles explicitly in the playbook.
cmds:
# roles/app/meta/main.yml
dependencies:
  - role: common
  - role: nginx
    vars:
      nginx_port: 8080
tip: Say explicit composition is clearer than hidden dependencies.

q: What are Ansible collections and how do you use and publish them?
a: A collection is a versioned package that can contain modules, plugins, roles, playbooks and docs under a namespace dot name identifier. Users install them with ansible-galaxy collection install, from Galaxy, Red Hat Automation Hub, a private Automation Hub or a Git repository, and list them in requirements.yml with version constraints. In playbooks you call content by its fully qualified collection name, or declare a collections search path. To publish, you create the skeleton with ansible-galaxy collection init, write a galaxy.yml with the namespace, name, version and dependencies, build with ansible-galaxy collection build, and publish the tarball with an API token. Teams often host internal collections in a private registry to share company roles, modules and filter plugins. I use semantic versioning, changelogs, sanity tests with ansible-test, and CI to build and release, and I pin consumers to a version range to avoid surprise breakages.
f: What goes in galaxy.yml?
How do you host a private collection?
p: A collection bundles modules, plugins and roles under a namespace and version. Install from Galaxy or a private hub via requirements.yml, call by fully qualified name, and publish with galaxy.yml, ansible-galaxy build and publish, with ansible-test in CI.
cmds: ansible-galaxy collection build && ansible-galaxy collection publish myorg-platform-1.2.0.tar.gz
tip: Say semantic versions and a pinned requirements file.

q: How do you use Galaxy and requirements.yml to manage dependencies reproducibly?
a: The requirements.yml file lists the roles and collections a project needs, with sources and versions, so anyone can install exactly the same content. For collections you give a name and a version constraint, and optionally a source or server, and for roles you can reference Galaxy names or Git URLs with a tag or commit. Installing is one command, and I set the collections and roles paths in ansible.cfg to a project-local directory, so nothing depends on what happens to be installed globally. For reproducibility I pin exact versions or narrow ranges, avoid tracking a moving branch in production, and use a private Automation Hub or mirror so builds do not depend on public availability. In CI, I install from the file in a clean environment before linting and testing. For enterprise setups, the same requirements file feeds ansible-builder to create an execution environment image, so the controller uses identical content.
f: Why avoid pinning to a branch?
How does requirements.yml feed an execution environment?
p: requirements.yml pins the roles and collections a project needs. Install into a project-local path, pin versions or commits, use a private mirror, and reuse the file to build execution environment images so every environment matches.
tip: Say pin versions and mirror privately for reproducibility.

q: When should logic be a role, a collection or a custom module?
a: I choose by what the reuse looks like. A role is the right unit to reuse a sequence of tasks that configures something, such as installing and configuring a service. A collection is the packaging and distribution layer: when I have several related roles, plugins or modules, or content shared across teams, I put them in a collection with versioning. A custom module is appropriate when the work needs real programming logic or an API that existing modules do not cover, or when a complex task in YAML becomes unreadable and not idempotent. Modules written in Python give structured arguments, check mode support, proper change detection and documentation, while a long chain of shell commands does not. Before writing anything new, I search existing collections, because maintained modules beat custom code. If I do write one, I test with ansible-test and unit tests and keep it small and well documented.
f: What makes a custom module better than a shell chain?
What does a module need to support check mode?
p: Use a role for reusable task sequences, a collection to package and version related content, and a custom module when you need real logic, an uncovered API, or proper idempotency and check mode. Search existing collections first.
tip: Say look for an existing module before writing one.

q: Why use fully qualified collection names, and how do you migrate old playbooks?
a: Fully qualified collection names, such as ansible.builtin.copy or amazon.aws.ec2_instance, remove ambiguity about which module runs. Without them, Ansible searches namespaces, and a collection added later could shadow a module of the same short name, changing behaviour silently. They also make it obvious where documentation and fixes live and which collection must be installed. Migration is mostly mechanical: ansible-lint has a fqcn rule that detects short names and can auto-fix many of them, and tools like the ansible-core migration notes list the mapping of old module names to collections. I update playbooks and roles, add the needed collections to requirements.yml with versions, run lint and Molecule, and test on a staging inventory. The effort is worth it because pinned, qualified content makes runs reproducible and upgrades of ansible-core much less risky. If the interviewer pushes further, I would explain how I would test this in a staging environment before touching production.
f: What can happen without FQCN when a new collection is installed?
How does ansible-lint help migrate?
p: FQCNs such as ansible.builtin.copy remove ambiguity and shadowing risk and show which collection is required. Migrate with ansible-lint fqcn rule, add collections to requirements.yml and test in staging.
tip: Say lint can auto-fix most short names.

q: How do you write a custom Ansible module, and what makes it good?
a: A custom module is usually a Python file placed in a library directory next to a playbook or role, or inside a collection. It uses the AnsibleModule helper to declare an argument specification with types, required flags, choices and defaults, reads the parameters, does the work, and exits with exit_json including changed and any result data, or fail_json with a message. A good module is idempotent: it checks the current state, compares to the desired state and changes only if needed. It supports check mode by declaring that and not applying changes, it never prints secrets, marks sensitive parameters with no_log, handles errors with clear messages, and includes documentation in the DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES and RETURN strings so ansible-doc works. I test with ansible-test sanity and units, and mock external calls. Module code runs on the target, so dependencies must be available there, otherwise consider an action plugin or a lookup running locally.
f: How do you support check mode?
How do you hide secret parameters?
p: Write a Python file using AnsibleModule with an argument spec, compute current versus desired state, return exit_json with changed, support check mode, use no_log for secrets, and document with DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES and RETURN. Test with ansible-test.
tip: Say idempotent, check-mode aware and documented.

q: What is the difference between role defaults and role vars, and how should you design role variables?
a: Role defaults, in defaults main, have the lowest precedence of all variables, so anything else can override them, inventory, play vars or the command line. They are meant for the public interface of the role: the knobs that users are expected to change, with sensible values. Role vars, in vars main, have high precedence and are hard to override, so they suit internal constants such as package names per operating system, which the user should not change. A good design puts every configurable setting in defaults, documents each in the README, prefixes names with the role name, such as nginx_worker_processes, and uses vars only for internal data or for values loaded per platform with include_vars. I avoid using vars for things users may need to override, because it frustrates them and leads to extra vars hacks. I also validate inputs with the assert module or an argument specification in the role meta, so mistakes fail early with a clear message.
f: What is an argument spec in role meta?
Why is overriding a role var difficult?
p: Defaults are lowest precedence and form the role's public, overridable interface. Vars are high precedence internals such as per-OS package names. Prefix names, document defaults and validate inputs with assert or an argument spec.
tip: Say defaults are the API, vars are the internals.

q: How do you write custom filter and lookup plugins, and when are they worthwhile?
a: Plugins extend what you can do in expressions and data lookups. A filter plugin is a Python file in a filter_plugins directory, or inside a collection, with a FilterModule class that returns a dictionary mapping filter names to functions, which you then use in Jinja2 like any built-in filter. A lookup plugin is a LookupModule class with a run method that receives terms and returns a list, running on the control node, so it can read local files, call APIs or query a secrets store. They are worthwhile when the same transformation or data fetch appears in many places and doing it in Jinja2 makes templates unreadable, for example normalising a CIDR list, parsing a vendor format, or retrieving a secret. Keep them small, pure where possible, documented and unit tested. Remember lookups run on the controller, not on the target, which affects file paths and credentials.
f: Where do lookup plugins execute?
Why keep filters pure?
p: A filter plugin is a Python class mapping names to functions used in Jinja2; a lookup plugin returns data from the control node. Use them to replace repeated or unreadable template logic, keep them small, tested and documented.
tip: Say lookups run on the controller, not on the target.

q: What are the ways to apply a role, and how do roles, import_role and include_role differ?
a: There are three ways. The roles keyword in a play applies roles statically before the play's tasks, in order, after pre_tasks. The import_role task statement is also static but lets you place the role anywhere among tasks, with tags and conditions applied to inner tasks at parse time. The include_role task statement is dynamic: it is evaluated when execution reaches it, so you can loop over it, pass variables computed at run time, or choose the role name from a variable, but tags need apply and the role contents are not visible in list-tasks. I use the roles keyword for the common simple case, import_role when I need ordering mixed with tasks, and include_role when the decision depends on facts or loops. I also use public true on include_role if I need its variables exposed to later tasks, since by default a dynamically included role's variables stay private.
f: When would you loop over include_role?
What does public true do?
p: The roles keyword applies roles statically before tasks; import_role is static anywhere in tasks; include_role is dynamic with loops and runtime names. Use public true to expose its variables.
tip: Say choose static for predictability, dynamic for runtime decisions.

q: Explain Ansible variable precedence and how to avoid surprises.
a: Ansible merges variables from many sources, and a defined order decides which wins. From lowest to highest, roughly: role defaults, inventory group variables, then host variables, playbook group_vars and host_vars, facts and registered variables, play vars and vars files, role vars, block and task vars, include parameters, set_fact, and finally extra vars passed with the e option, which beat everything. The documentation lists about twenty-two levels, and the key mental model is that more specific and more explicit sources win. To avoid surprises I keep variables in few places: role defaults for knobs, group_vars and host_vars for environment data, and extra vars only for exceptional overrides or CI parameters. I prefix names with the role, avoid reusing names across layers, and avoid set_fact for configuration because it overrides most things. When debugging, the debug module with var set to the name, or the vars magic variable and the ansible-inventory host output, shows the final value.
f: Why do extra vars beat everything?
How do you find where a variable value came from?
p: Variables merge from defaults, inventory, group and host vars, facts, play vars, role vars, task vars, set_fact and extra vars, with more specific and explicit sources winning. Keep variables in few places, prefix names and debug with ansible-inventory and the debug module.
tip: Say defaults for knobs, group_vars for environments, extra vars for exceptions.

q: How do you organise group_vars and host_vars for multiple environments?
a: I lay out the inventory so environments are separate and shared data is not duplicated. A common structure is one inventory directory per environment, such as production and staging, each with its own hosts file or dynamic source and its own group_vars and host_vars directories, plus an all group file for global values. Within group_vars I create a directory per group containing several small files, for example vars.yml for ordinary values and vault.yml for encrypted ones, which keeps secrets separate and diffs readable. Roles hold defaults, groups such as webservers and databases hold role-specific settings, and environment directories hold environment-specific settings like endpoints and sizes. I avoid duplicating the same value across environments by placing it in a shared group, and I avoid very deep group hierarchies since precedence between sibling groups at the same level is by alphabetical order, which is fragile. A prefix convention helps with the vault variables and their plain references.
f: Why split vars.yml and vault.yml?
What decides precedence between two groups at the same depth?
p: Use one inventory directory per environment with group_vars and host_vars, a group directory with vars.yml and vault.yml, shared values in an all group, and avoid deep hierarchies where precedence is fragile.
cmds:
inventories/
  production/
    hosts.yml
    group_vars/all/vars.yml
    group_vars/db/vault.yml
  staging/
tip: Say separate plain and vault files per group.

q: How do Jinja2 templates work in Ansible and what are good practices?
a: The template module renders a Jinja2 file on the control node using the host's variables and copies the result to the target. Jinja2 provides expressions in double curly braces, statements such as for loops and if conditions in curly percent tags, filters, tests and comments. Templates are used to generate configuration files such as nginx, systemd units or application properties. Good practices: keep logic simple in templates and compute complex data in tasks or filters; add a managed-by header with the ansible_managed variable so people know not to edit by hand; use validate to check syntax with the service's own tool before replacing the file; set owner, group and mode; use trim_blocks and lstrip_blocks to control whitespace; use the default filter and the mandatory filter to handle missing values deliberately; and never put secrets in templated files that are logged or diffed, using no_log. Test rendering with check and diff.
f: What does the validate parameter do?
How do you control whitespace in templates?
p: The template module renders Jinja2 on the controller with host variables. Keep logic simple, add an ansible_managed header, use validate before replacing, set mode and owner, use defaults and mandatory deliberately, and avoid exposing secrets.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    mode: '0644'
    validate: 'nginx -t -c %s'
tip: Say validate and ansible_managed.

q: Which Jinja2 filters do you use most in Ansible, and for what?
a: A few filters cover most needs. The default filter provides a fallback when a variable is undefined, and with true as a second argument also for empty values. The mandatory filter fails loudly if a value is missing. For data shaping, I use map and select with attribute to extract fields from lists of dictionaries, selectattr and rejectattr to filter, join, split, unique, sort, flatten and zip. The combine filter merges dictionaries, optionally recursively, dict2items and items2dict convert between formats, and json_query uses JMESPath for nested queries. For strings and security, regex_replace and regex_search, b64encode, password_hash and the quote filter for shell safety. For networking, the ansible.utils ipaddr and ipaddr style filters handle addresses and subnets. Type filters like int, bool and list handle strings coming from the command line. I keep expressions short, and when a filter chain becomes long I compute it in a set_fact or a custom filter for readability.
f: How do you merge two dictionaries?
What does selectattr do?
p: Key filters: default and mandatory, map, select, selectattr, join, unique, combine, dict2items, json_query, regex_replace, quote and type conversions. Keep chains short and move complex logic into set_fact or a custom filter.
tip: Say default, mandatory, combine and selectattr are the workhorses.

q: How do register, set_fact and magic variables like hostvars work together?
a: The register keyword saves a task's result into a variable, containing fields such as stdout, rc, changed and, for loops, a results list. The set_fact module creates or updates a variable for the current host at run time, which persists for the rest of the play, and can be cached across plays if fact caching is enabled. Magic variables are provided by Ansible: inventory_hostname, group_names, groups, play_hosts, ansible_play_batch, and hostvars, a dictionary giving access to variables and facts of any other host in the inventory. Together they let one host's play use data from others, for example a web server reading the database host's address from hostvars of the first host in the db group. Cautions: hostvars facts exist only if that host has already been contacted in the run, set_fact has high precedence, which can mask configuration, and registered variables from skipped tasks still exist with a skipped flag, so check before using the output.
f: When does hostvars not contain facts for another host?
Why is set_fact risky for configuration?
p: register captures task output, set_fact defines run-time variables per host, and magic variables like hostvars, groups and inventory_hostname expose inventory and other hosts. Beware hostvars before facts are gathered, set_fact precedence and skipped registered results.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.command: hostname -f
  register: fqdn
- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    db_host: "{{ hostvars[groups['db'][0]].ansible_default_ipv4.address }}"
tip: Say hostvars needs facts already gathered for that host.

q: What are lookup plugins and how do you use them safely?
a: Lookups retrieve data from external sources during templating and run on the control node, not on the target. Common ones read files, environment variables, URLs, DNS records, CSV or INI files, password generation, and secret stores such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and 1Password through collections. They are called with the lookup function, or the query function, which always returns a list. Safe use means remembering the controller location, for example a file lookup reads from the machine running Ansible, not the target. For secrets, I prefer a lookup against a dedicated secrets manager with short-lived credentials over storing values in vars files, and I set no_log on tasks that use them so the value is not printed. Because lookups run at each evaluation of a variable, an expensive one used in many places can slow down a play, so I register the result once or wrap it in set_fact. I also handle missing items with the default or errors ignore options.
f: What is the difference between lookup and query?
Why might a lookup be slow in a template?
p: Lookups fetch data on the control node from files, env, URLs, DNS or secret stores. Use query for lists, protect output with no_log, and evaluate expensive lookups once with set_fact. Remember paths are controller paths.
tip: Say lookups run on the controller and should be no_log when secret.

q: How do you generate configuration from structured data using loops in templates?
a: I model the data as variables in YAML, for example a list of virtual hosts or a dictionary of upstreams, then render with a for loop in the template. Inside Jinja2 a for loop can iterate lists and dictionary items, with loop.index, loop.first and loop.last helpers for commas or separators, and conditional blocks for optional settings. For cleaner output I use trim_blocks and lstrip_blocks, and I avoid putting complicated logic in the template by preparing data with filters in the task, for example sorting, grouping or merging defaults with overrides using combine. For files that are one resource per file, I loop at the task level with the template module and set the destination from the item, which makes handlers and permissions simpler. Testing is by rendering with check and diff, and by validating the output with the service's own syntax checker. Keeping the data model separate from the template means non-experts can add a host by editing YAML.
f: When would you loop in the task instead of the template?
How do you avoid trailing commas in generated files?
p: Model data as YAML, loop in Jinja2 with loop.first and loop.last helpers, prepare data with filters or combine, and use task-level loops for one-file-per-item cases. Validate generated files with the service's checker.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.template:
    src: vhost.j2
    dest: "/etc/nginx/conf.d/{{ item.name }}.conf"
  loop: "{{ vhosts }}"
tip: Say separate the data model from the template.

q: How do you merge default and override dictionaries, and what are the pitfalls?
a: The combine filter merges dictionaries, with the right side winning on key conflicts. By default it is shallow, so a nested dictionary on the right replaces the entire nested dictionary on the left. With recursive true it merges nested keys, and the list_merge option controls what happens with lists: replace, append, prepend or keep. A typical pattern is a role default dictionary, such as app_config_defaults, combined with a user-supplied app_config_overrides, into a final value in a task or template. Pitfalls include accidental shallow merges that drop nested defaults, ordering mistakes where the wrong side wins, lists that are replaced rather than extended, and variable precedence, since a dictionary defined at multiple levels is replaced, not merged, unless hash_behaviour merge is enabled, which is discouraged and deprecated. I therefore use explicit combine in code with documented variable names, rather than relying on global merge behaviour.
f: Why is hash_behaviour merge discouraged?
How do you append lists when merging?
p: Use combine, with recursive true for nested dictionaries and list_merge to control lists. Keep defaults and overrides as separate variables, and avoid global hash_behaviour merge since precedence otherwise replaces whole dictionaries.
tip: Say variables replace by default, so combine explicitly.

q: What is Ansible Vault and how do you use it?
a: Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive data, such as passwords, keys and tokens, so it can be stored in version control. You can encrypt a whole file with ansible-vault encrypt, create one with create, edit with edit, and view with view. Alternatively, you can encrypt a single value with encrypt_string, which produces a vault tag inline in a YAML file, so the rest of the file stays readable in diffs. Playbooks decrypt transparently at run time when you provide a password through a prompt, a file, or a script with the vault-password-file option or the ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE variable. It uses AES-256 with a key derived from the password. Practices: keep encrypted variables in a separate vault.yml and reference them from plain variables named with a vault prefix so people can grep names; never commit the password file; rotate with rekey; and for larger organisations use an external secrets manager so that rotation and auditing are handled centrally.
f: Whole-file versus inline encryption: which do you prefer?
How do you rotate the vault password?
p: Vault encrypts files or single strings with AES-256 so secrets can live in git. Supply the password through a file or script, keep encrypted variables in a separate vault.yml referenced by plain names, rekey to rotate, and consider an external secrets manager at scale.
tip: Say never commit the password file.

q: How do vault IDs work and how do you use multiple vault passwords?
a: Vault IDs label encrypted content so you can use different passwords for different environments or teams, for example dev, prod and shared. When encrypting, you pass vault-id with a label and a source, such as prod at a prompt, a file, or a script. The label is stored in the vault header. At run time you can supply several vault-id options, each with its own source, and Ansible tries the matching label first, then others. This allows developers to hold the dev password while only the pipeline or a few engineers hold the production one, so a developer can run against staging without being able to decrypt production secrets. A script as the source can fetch the password from a secrets manager or a keychain, which avoids files on disk. Pitfalls: the label is a hint, not a security boundary by itself, so access control to the actual passwords is what matters, and rotating requires rekeying each ID.
f: What does the label in the header do?
How would a script supply the password?
p: Vault IDs label encrypted content, so different environments use different passwords. Provide several vault-id sources at run time; Ansible matches the label. Use scripts to fetch passwords from a secrets manager and limit who holds the production one.
tip: Say the label is not a security boundary; password access is.

q: How do you integrate Ansible with HashiCorp Vault or cloud secret managers instead of using Ansible Vault?
a: For larger environments, a dedicated secrets manager gives central access control, audit, rotation and dynamic short-lived credentials, which file-based Vault cannot. Ansible integrates through lookup plugins, for instance the hashi_vault lookup in the community.hashi_vault collection, the aws_secret lookup in amazon.aws, or equivalents for Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager. The control node, or the AWX execution environment, authenticates with a short-lived method: AppRole, Kubernetes auth, OIDC or cloud instance identity, rather than a static token. Lookups fetch values at run time, and tasks that use them set no_log true. In AWX or Ansible Automation Platform, credential types can inject secrets from an external credential source so job templates never store the secret. Considerations: the lookup runs on the controller, so network access to the secrets manager is needed there, failures should stop the run clearly, and values should not be cached in facts or written to logs.
f: Why prefer short-lived authentication methods?
Where does a lookup run in AWX?
p: Use lookup plugins for HashiCorp Vault, AWS, Azure or GCP secret managers, authenticate with short-lived identities such as AppRole, OIDC or instance identity, set no_log, and in AWX use external credential sources so secrets are not stored in job templates.
tip: Say no static tokens and no_log on the task.

q: What does no_log do, and how else do you keep secrets out of logs and output?
a: Setting no_log true on a task or play hides its arguments and results from output, logs and callbacks, replacing them with a notice, which prevents passwords and tokens from appearing in the console, in AWX job output or in CI logs. It also hides useful debugging information, so I enable it only on tasks that handle secrets, and keep it off in a debug build with a variable. Other protections: mark module parameters as no_log in custom modules, avoid passing secrets on command lines where they show in process lists, use environment variables or files with strict permissions, avoid the debug module on secret variables, be careful with verbose flags since they can reveal data, and exclude secrets from check and diff output with diff false on tasks that template secret files. Callback plugins and external logging should be reviewed, and CI systems should mask variables. Also remember that registered results can contain secrets, so avoid printing them.
f: How can a secret leak through diff mode?
Why avoid secrets on command lines?
p: no_log hides task arguments and results from output and logs. Use it only where needed, avoid command-line secrets, disable diff on secret templates, mask CI variables and avoid printing registered results.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: https://api/login
    body: {password: "{{ api_pass }}"}
  no_log: true

- ansible.builtin.template:
    src: secrets.j2
    dest: /etc/app/secrets
    diff: false
tip: Say no_log hides debugging too, so scope it.

q: How do you secure SSH access and key management for Ansible?
a: Ansible's security is largely SSH security. I use a dedicated automation account on the targets, key-based authentication only, with passwords disabled, and a key per environment or per controller rather than a shared personal key. Keys are held in an agent or a secrets manager, not copied around, and protected with passphrases where a human is involved. On targets, the authorized key can be restricted with options such as from, command or no-port-forwarding when feasible, and sudo is limited through a sudoers file to what is required. Better still, use short-lived SSH certificates issued by a certificate authority such as Vault's SSH secrets engine, so there are no long-lived keys to rotate. Host key checking stays enabled, with known hosts populated by trusted means, not disabled globally, which would allow man-in-the-middle attacks. Access to private networks goes through a hardened bastion with ProxyJump or ProxyCommand and audit logging.
f: Why not disable host key checking?
What is an SSH certificate and why use one?
p: Use a dedicated automation account with key-only auth, per-environment keys or short-lived SSH certificates, restricted sudo, host key checking enabled and a hardened, audited bastion for private networks.
tip: Say short-lived SSH certificates beat long-lived keys.

q: How do you use Ansible for security hardening and compliance, such as CIS benchmarks?
a: Ansible suits hardening because it applies and verifies a desired baseline consistently. I start from maintained content, such as the community dev-sec hardening collection or the CIS and DISA STIG roles, and adapt them rather than writing every control by hand. Controls cover SSH configuration, password and account policy, file permissions, kernel parameters, services disabled, auditd and logging, firewall rules and package updates. Each control gets a tag and a variable to enable or exempt it, with documented justifications for exceptions. I run in check mode with diff for an assessment, then in apply mode in stages, starting with staging and a canary group, since some hardening, like restricting SSH or mounting options, can lock people out or break applications. After applying, scanners such as OpenSCAP or InSpec verify compliance and produce reports for auditors. Results are scheduled to detect drift, with the playbook run from AWX on a timer.
f: How do you avoid locking yourself out?
How do you prove compliance to auditors?
p: Start from maintained hardening roles, make controls tagged and toggleable with documented exceptions, assess in check mode, apply in stages with a canary group, verify with OpenSCAP or InSpec, and schedule runs to catch drift.
tip: Say staged rollout, verification scan and exceptions with reasons.

q: How do you design privilege escalation and sudo policy for automation accounts?
a: The aim is that automation can do what it needs and nothing more. I create a dedicated automation user per purpose and per environment, with key-based login, and grant it sudo through a file in the sudoers directory, validated with visudo. The broadest option is passwordless sudo for all commands, which is convenient but means that compromise of the controller equals root everywhere. A tighter policy limits sudo to specific commands, or uses separate accounts for specific roles, for example an application deployment account that may restart one service. Where full root is required, I protect the controller strongly: restricted access, audit logging, short-lived credentials and network segmentation. In playbooks I apply become only to the tasks that need it, and use become_user with an application account for file ownership. Sudo logging and session auditing record what was run. I review these policies regularly and test that playbooks still work under the restricted policy in staging.
f: What is the risk of passwordless sudo ALL?
How do you validate a sudoers file safely?
p: Use dedicated automation accounts with key login and sudoers entries validated by visudo. Prefer command-limited sudo where practical, protect the controller strongly if root is needed, apply become only to needed tasks and audit sudo activity.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.copy:
    dest: /etc/sudoers.d/ansible
    content: "ansible ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart app\n"
    validate: 'visudo -cf %s'
    mode: '0440'
tip: Say the controller becomes the crown jewel if sudo is broad.

q: How do you handle secrets in CI/CD pipelines that run Ansible?
a: The pipeline needs secrets, but they should be short-lived, scoped and never printed. I store the vault password or the cloud credentials in the CI system's secret store, expose them only to protected branches and environments, and have the job write the vault password to a temporary file with strict permissions or pass it through a script, removing it afterwards. Better, the job authenticates to a secrets manager with an OIDC identity from the CI provider, retrieving short-lived credentials at run time, which avoids stored long-lived secrets. SSH keys are loaded into an agent for the job's duration only. Logs are protected with masking and no_log, and verbosity is not enabled on production runs. For pull requests from forks, secrets are not exposed. Production runs need approvals, and the same pipeline uses a separate credential set per environment. Finally, audit logs show who triggered what, and credentials are rotated on a schedule.
f: How does OIDC avoid stored secrets in CI?
Why not expose secrets to fork pull requests?
p: Keep secrets in the CI secret store scoped to protected branches, prefer OIDC to fetch short-lived credentials, write vault passwords to temporary files and remove them, load SSH keys into an agent only per job, mask logs and require approval for production.
tip: Say OIDC short-lived credentials beat stored secrets.

q: How do you audit and review Ansible code for security problems?
a: I treat playbooks as code that can change production, so they get review and automated checks. ansible-lint runs in CI with a profile such as production, catching risky patterns: use of shell where a module exists, missing no_log, world-writable file modes, plain-text passwords, unpinned package versions and missing FQCNs. Secret scanning tools like gitleaks or trufflehog check commits for credentials. Code review focuses on privilege, on tasks that download and execute remote content, disabled certificate validation, disabled host key checking, and templates that embed secrets. Branch protection requires approval for production playbooks, with separate reviewers for sensitive roles. At run time, AWX or the platform provides audit logs of who ran which job template with which inputs, and I forward them to the central logging system. Dependencies are scanned too, as roles and collections from public sources can be compromised, so I pin versions and mirror trusted content.
f: Which lint rules catch security problems?
How do you protect against malicious Galaxy content?
p: Run ansible-lint with a strict profile and secret scanning in CI, review privilege, downloads, disabled validation and secrets, protect production branches, keep AWX audit logs centrally, and pin and mirror third-party roles and collections.
tip: Say pin and mirror third-party content.

q: How do extra vars, vars_files and include_vars differ, and when do you use each?
a: Extra vars, passed with the e option on the command line or from a file, have the highest precedence and override everything else, so I use them for run-specific parameters from a pipeline or an operator, such as a version to deploy or a target environment, and never for ordinary configuration. A vars_files entry in a play loads variables from listed files when the play starts, handy for a fixed set of environment data. The include_vars module loads a file or directory dynamically during execution, so the file name can depend on facts, for example an OS-specific variables file per distribution, with the loaded values taking task-level precedence. I use include_vars with first_found to select a file such as the OS family and falling back to a default. Care points: extra vars arrive as strings, so booleans and numbers need type conversion; large extra vars from untrusted users can be dangerous, so I restrict them in AWX with surveys and validation.
f: Why do extra vars arrive as strings?
How would you load OS-specific variables?
p: Extra vars have the highest precedence and suit run-time parameters; vars_files loads fixed files at play start; include_vars loads dynamically, for example per OS with first_found. Convert types and restrict inputs in AWX surveys.
tip: Say extra vars for parameters, not for configuration.

q: How do you validate inputs and variables so a playbook fails early with clear messages?
a: Failing early saves time and prevents half-applied changes. Within a play I use the assert module at the start with conditions and custom fail messages, for example checking that a required variable is defined, a port is in range, a version string matches a pattern, or a list is not empty. The mandatory filter and the default filter used carefully also catch missing values. For roles, the argument_specs file in the role meta directory defines types, required flags, choices and defaults for each entry point, and Ansible validates inputs before the role runs, producing a clear error and doubling as documentation. At the boundary with users, AWX surveys can restrict choices and types. I also run pre-flight checks for connectivity, disk space and package repository access in pre_tasks, so problems are found before changes start. This makes failures cheap, predictable and easy to understand for the person who ran the job.
f: What does argument_specs give you?
What belongs in a pre-flight check?
p: Use assert with clear messages, the mandatory filter, role argument_specs for typed validation, AWX surveys and pre-flight tasks for connectivity and capacity, so a bad input fails before any change.
cmds:
- ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - app_version is match('^[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+$')
      - app_port | int in range(1024, 65536)
    fail_msg: 'Invalid app_version or app_port'
tip: Say fail early with a human-readable message.

q: How do you rotate secrets and the vault password with minimal disruption?
a: Rotation should be routine, not an emergency. For Ansible Vault content, the rekey command re-encrypts files with a new password, and with vault IDs you can rotate one environment at a time. The process is: generate the new password in the secrets manager, rekey all encrypted files in a branch, update the pipeline and the controller's secret to the new value, merge, and then revoke the old one, ideally keeping a short overlap during which both work. For application secrets stored in vault files, rotation means changing the secret at the source, such as the database user, and then updating the encrypted value and redeploying, which can be automated with a playbook that updates both ends in a safe order, avoiding downtime by supporting two credentials during the transition. Moving the application secrets to an external secrets manager with dynamic credentials reduces the manual work. I record rotation dates and test the process regularly, including recovery.
f: How do you rekey many files at once?
How do you avoid downtime during a database password change?
p: Rekey vault files with ansible-vault rekey, rotate per vault ID, update pipeline secrets and revoke the old password after an overlap. For application secrets, rotate at the source, support two credentials during transition and consider a secrets manager with dynamic credentials.
tip: Say plan an overlap, then revoke the old secret.

q: How do forks affect performance, and how do you tune them?
a: The forks setting controls how many hosts Ansible works on in parallel for each task, defaulting to five, which is conservative. Raising it speeds up runs across large inventories, since more hosts are contacted at once, but it consumes more memory and CPU on the control node and more simultaneous SSH connections, so there is a limit set by the controller's resources and by the targets and any jump hosts or bastions, which may have connection limits. I tune by measuring: increase forks in steps, such as 20, 50 and 100, watch controller load and memory, and the task timings, and stop where improvement flattens. Forks apply per task across the current batch, so with the serial keyword the effective parallelism is limited to the batch size. Other settings interact: SSH pipelining, ControlPersist, fact gathering, and the strategy. For very large fleets, I also distribute the work across several controllers or AWX execution nodes instead of one big machine.
f: What limits forks in practice?
How does serial interact with forks?
p: Forks sets parallel hosts per task, default five. Raise it stepwise while watching controller CPU, memory and bastion limits, remember serial caps batch size, and for very large fleets spread work across multiple execution nodes.
tip: Say measure, increase gradually and watch the controller.

q: What are the linear, free and other strategies, and when do you use them?
a: A strategy decides how tasks are scheduled across hosts. The default linear strategy runs each task on all hosts in the batch and waits for the slowest before starting the next task, which keeps hosts in lockstep and is predictable. The free strategy lets each host proceed through the tasks as fast as it can without waiting, which shortens total time when hosts differ in speed, but output is interleaved and ordering assumptions between hosts, such as one host depending on another having finished a step, break. The host_pinned strategy is similar to free but keeps a worker on a host. The debug strategy drops into an interactive debugger on failure. I use linear for coordinated rollouts and anything with cross-host dependencies, and free for independent work such as patching or package installation across many unrelated servers. The strategy is set per play, and I combine it with serial for rolling control.
f: Why can free break dependencies between hosts?
What does the debug strategy do?
p: Linear keeps hosts in lockstep and is predictable; free lets each host run ahead for speed when tasks are independent; host_pinned and debug are variants. Use linear for coordinated changes and free for independent bulk work.
tip: Say free is faster but loses ordering guarantees.

q: How do you do rolling updates with serial, and control failures during them?
a: The serial keyword limits how many hosts a play works on at a time, so the whole play, all tasks, finishes for one batch before the next batch starts. It can be a number, a percentage or a list that grows, such as 1, then 5, then 20, which gives a canary pattern: one host first, then more. Combined with max_fail_percentage and any_errors_fatal it stops the rollout if too many hosts fail, protecting the remaining healthy servers. Typical flow for a web tier: remove a host from the load balancer with a delegated task, update, run health checks, return it to service, then move to the next batch. I add a wait_for or uri check after each update, so a bad host fails the batch immediately. Note that with serial, run_once applies per batch, and that variable max_fail_percentage applies to each batch. Set batches so capacity remains sufficient while hosts are out.
f: What is a growing serial list?
How do you pick a safe batch size?
p: serial limits a play to batches, which gives rolling updates and canary patterns with a growing list. Add max_fail_percentage or any_errors_fatal and health checks so a failing batch stops the rollout; keep enough capacity while batches are out.
tip: Say canary first batch plus health checks and a failure threshold.

q: How do SSH pipelining, ControlPersist and Mitogen speed up Ansible?
a: By default Ansible opens a connection and runs several SSH operations per task, such as creating a temporary directory, copying the module, executing it and cleaning up. Enabling ControlPersist, which is on by default with OpenSSH, keeps a master connection open and reuses it, avoiding repeated handshakes. Enabling pipelining in ansible.cfg sends the module code over the existing SSH session rather than writing a temporary file first, cutting the number of round trips substantially, with one caveat: it requires that requiretty is not set in sudoers on targets. ControlPath length can also cause issues on long hostnames. Mitogen for Ansible is a third-party strategy plugin that replaces the connection and execution layer with a persistent, multiplexed process, which can give large speedups, but it lags behind newer ansible-core releases and is not supported in managed platforms, so it is a decision with trade-offs. I measure with the profile_tasks callback before and after changes.
f: What does pipelining require on the target?
How do you measure which tasks are slow?
p: ControlPersist reuses SSH connections and pipelining sends modules over the existing session, cutting round trips, provided requiretty is off. Mitogen can speed things further but has compatibility trade-offs. Measure with profile_tasks.
tip: Say measure with profile_tasks before and after.

q: How do fact caching and limiting fact gathering help at scale?
a: Gathering facts runs the setup module on every host at the start of each play, which for thousands of hosts and several plays costs a lot of time. I reduce this in layers. First, disable gathering in plays that do not need facts. Second, use gather_subset to collect only needed categories, such as min. Third, enable a fact cache with the smart gathering policy and a backend such as Redis, memcached or JSON files, with a timeout, so facts from a recent run are reused and not recomputed. With caching, other hosts' facts remain available through hostvars even when a play targets only a subset, which helps cross-host templating. The cost is staleness: facts can be old, so the timeout should match how quickly the data changes, and tasks that need fresh values, such as disk usage, should refresh explicitly or avoid the cache. Redis gives shared caching for several controllers.
f: What does the smart gathering policy do?
What data should not come from a cache?
p: Disable or subset fact gathering, and enable a fact cache such as Redis or JSON with smart gathering and a timeout so recent facts are reused. Watch staleness and refresh volatile facts explicitly.
cmds:
[defaults]
gathering = smart
fact_caching = redis
fact_caching_timeout = 3600
fact_caching_connection = redis01:6379:0
tip: Say pick a timeout matching how fast facts change.

q: How do async and poll work, and when do you use them for long-running tasks?
a: By default Ansible holds an SSH connection open until a task finishes, which can time out on long operations such as large package upgrades, database dumps or reboots. With async you set a maximum runtime in seconds, and poll sets how often Ansible checks. With a poll interval greater than zero, Ansible still waits but uses a background job and polling, avoiding connection timeouts. With poll set to zero it starts the job and moves on immediately, which lets you fire a task on many hosts, run other work, and later collect the results with the async_status module and the job id from the registered variable. This is useful for parallelising slow tasks, for starting several long jobs across hosts and checking them afterwards.
